explanations.explanation: Paul, the writer of this letter, says, "I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles..." (Ephesians 3:1). Most of us lead with a job title, friend. I'd print "Master Stamper" on my business card in gold ink and hand out fifty of them. Paul leads with prisoner, and he says it's for the sake of the Gentiles.

Shepherd is a lovely title, but it's not the one Paul, the writer of this letter, picks here. His words are, "I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles..." (Ephesians 3:1). No flock anywhere in that line. I think shepherd would sound smoother, but Paul went with prisoner.

Builder is a strong title, and I'd put it on a business card in a heartbeat. But Paul, the writer of this letter, doesn't use it here. He says, "I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles..." (Ephesians 3:1). Nothing about building in that line, friend.

Paul writes, "the mystery made known to me by revelation" (Ephesians 3:3). Made known to him. That means it was shown to him, not dug up by him. I've read a lot of recipe cards in my day, and not one of them ever arrived by revelation.

Studying is a fine thing, friend, but that's not what Paul says here. He writes, "the mystery made known to me by revelation" (Ephesians 3:3). The mystery was made known to him. He doesn't say he worked it out himself.
Paul doesn't name the other apostles as his source in this verse. He says, "the mystery made known to me by revelation" (Ephesians 3:3). Revelation is the word he uses. Keep your eyes on that one.

Paul says it right there: "as I have already written briefly." (Ephesians 3:3). So this isn't the first time he's brought it up. He's circling back to it. I do the same thing with a good dough recipe, and I only wrote mine on the back of a flour sack.

This one is true, friend. Paul says, "as I have already written briefly." (Ephesians 3:3). He has already written about the mystery, and he's coming back to it. He doesn't say he's never mentioned it.

Paul says it has "now been revealed by the Spirit to God's holy apostles and prophets." (Ephesians 3:5). The Spirit is the One doing the revealing. Notice that it says holy apostles and prophets, so Paul is not the only one in the picture.

Kings would get the royal treatment at my bakery, but they're not who Paul names here. He says the mystery was revealed by the Spirit "to God's holy apostles and prophets." (Ephesians 3:5). No crowns in that verse, friend.

Paul doesn't mention priests here. He says the mystery was revealed by the Spirit "to God's holy apostles and prophets." (Ephesians 3:5). Apostles and prophets, that's the list. I'd stick to the list.

explanations.answer: They are fellow heirs in Christ Jesus
explanations.explanation: Paul says the Gentiles "are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus." (Ephesians 3:6). Heirs, friend. A guest eats one cookie and heads home, but an heir shares in what's been handed down. That's what Paul is saying about the Gentiles.

explanations.answer: They are guests at Israel's table
explanations.explanation: Guests is a nice try, but Paul uses a bigger word. He says the Gentiles "are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus." (Ephesians 3:6). A guest visits, and a fellow heir shares in the inheritance. Paul says fellow heirs.

explanations.answer: They are servants to God's people
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing about servants here. Three times he says fellow: "fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus." (Ephesians 3:6). Fellow means alongside. Nobody gets handed an apron and told to stay in the back.

Paul says the opposite. The Gentiles are "fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus." (Ephesians 3:6). Fellow partakers means they share in it with everyone else. He doesn't describe a smaller share anywhere in this verse.

Right, friend. Paul says the Gentiles are "fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus." (Ephesians 3:6). Fellow partakers, so they share in it with everyone else. Not one word about a smaller share.
Paul writes, "I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God's grace" (Ephesians 3:7). A gift, friend. He doesn't say he earned the job. I love a gift that comes with no receipt to return.

Law is a big word in the Bible, but it's not the one Paul uses here. He says, "I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God's grace" (Ephesians 3:7). It came as a gift of grace. That's the word that fits the blank.

Covenant is a strong word, but it doesn't go in this blank. Paul says, "I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God's grace" (Ephesians 3:7). He calls it a gift of grace. That's the one that fits.
It's the opposite, friend. Paul says, "Though I am less than the least of all the saints..." (Ephesians 3:8). He doesn't put himself at the top. He puts himself below the bottom.
That's right. Paul says, "Though I am less than the least of all the saints..." (Ephesians 3:8). He's not at the top of that list. I think that's the humblest résumé line ever written.

Paul says he was given grace "to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ" (Ephesians 3:8). Unsearchable, friend. That means you can't reach the bottom of them. I've tried to reach the bottom of a cookie jar, and even that has an end.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, but Paul doesn't bring him up here. He says he was given grace "to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ" (Ephesians 3:8). The riches of Christ are his message. That's the whole job in that verse.

Solomon, Israel's king, is a famous name, but Paul doesn't mention him here. He says he was given grace "to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ" (Ephesians 3:8). It's all about Christ's riches. Nothing else is on the list.

explanations.answer: In God who created all things
explanations.explanation: Paul says it "for ages past was kept hidden in God, who created all things." (Ephesians 3:9). It was hidden in God, friend. Now Paul's job is to shine a light on it. I'd say a light is a better thing to have than a dusty drawer.

explanations.answer: In the scrolls of the prophets
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, but it's not what Paul says. He says it "for ages past was kept hidden in God, who created all things." (Ephesians 3:9). The place is God, not scrolls. Stick with Paul's words.
Paul doesn't mention the temple here. He says it "for ages past was kept hidden in God, who created all things." (Ephesians 3:9). It was hidden in God. That's the place Paul names.

explanations.answer: The rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "His purpose was that now, through the church, the manifold wisdom of God should be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms." (Ephesians 3:10). The heavenly realms, friend. That audience is a lot bigger than my little bakery crowd. I'd bake an extra batch.

explanations.answer: The kings and judges of all the earth
explanations.explanation: Earth's kings and judges aren't the audience Paul names. He says the wisdom of God should be made known "to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms." (Ephesians 3:10). Heavenly realms. That's a different address than any palace on earth.

explanations.answer: The elders and priests of the house of Israel
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't name elders or priests here. He says the wisdom of God should be made known "to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms." (Ephesians 3:10). The audience is in the heavenly realms. Read that part twice if you need to.

Paul says it was "the eternal purpose that He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord." (Ephesians 3:11). Eternal, friend. That means it was never a rush job. I've had plenty of recipes I had to rush, and I don't recommend it.
This one is true. Paul says it was "the eternal purpose that He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord." (Ephesians 3:11). The word is right there. Eternal purpose.

Paul says the opposite. "In Him and through faith in Him we may enter God's presence with boldness and confidence." (Ephesians 3:12). Boldness and confidence, not fear and hesitation. Nobody has to tiptoe in.

That's right. Paul says, "In Him and through faith in Him we may enter God's presence with boldness and confidence." (Ephesians 3:12). The way in is through Christ and through faith in Him. Boldness and confidence are the words he picks.

explanations.answer: Not to be discouraged by them
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "So I ask you not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory." (Ephesians 3:13). That's his request, friend. I think it's the kind of thing a good dad would say. He's in a hard spot, and he's still thinking about them.

explanations.answer: To come and visit him soon
explanations.explanation: A visit would be nice, but that's not what Paul asks for here. He says, "So I ask you not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory." (Ephesians 3:13). His request is about their hearts. He asks them not to be discouraged.

Paul doesn't ask for that in this verse. He says, "So I ask you not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory." (Ephesians 3:13). His request is that they not be discouraged. That's the ask.

Paul says it right at the end of the verse: "my sufferings for you, which are your glory." (Ephesians 3:13). Your glory, friend. I won't pretend to explain more than he does there. I'll just say he said it, and he said it kindly.
This one is true. Paul says, "my sufferings for you, which are your glory." (Ephesians 3:13). Those last three words are the answer. Your glory.
